title: Introduction to DevOps
description: Understand the culture, lifecycle, and feedback loops that help teams ship reliable software with less drama.

topics.title: Principles and culture of DevOps
topics.definition: DevOps combines development and operations practices so teams can deliver software more often and operate it reliably.
topics.why: Shared responsibility and shorter feedback loops help teams find problems before they become expensive incidents.
topics.how: A small change moves through version control, automated checks, a controlled release, and monitoring. The team learns from the result and improves the next loop.
topics.example: A developer commits a change, a pipeline runs tests, and monitoring confirms whether the release behaves as expected.
topics.mistake: Treating DevOps as one tool or one job title. The useful part is the working agreement between people, process, and technology.
topics.recap: DevOps is a way of working: shared ownership, automation, fast feedback, and continuous improvement.

topics.title: DevOps engineer skills and career scope
topics.definition: A DevOps engineer helps automate building, testing, deployment, infrastructure, and system operations.
topics.why: The role connects software delivery with the systems that keep software available and safe.
topics.how: Begin with Linux, networking, Git, scripting, and cloud basics. Then add containers, CI/CD, infrastructure as code, monitoring, and security.
topics.example: A learner may start by writing a shell script, then use it in a CI job, and later turn the same workflow into reusable infrastructure code.
topics.mistake: Collecting many tools before learning the underlying concepts. Fundamentals transfer across vendors; product names change.
topics.recap: Strong DevOps careers grow from fundamentals, curiosity, and communication as much as from tool knowledge.

topics.title: DevOps lifecycle and delivery pipeline
topics.definition: The lifecycle commonly includes plan, code, build, test, release, deploy, operate, and monitor.
topics.why: A visible lifecycle makes handoffs, ownership, and improvement opportunities easier to discuss.
topics.how: A pipeline automates repeatable steps and provides evidence that a change is ready. The stages form a feedback loop rather than a one-way line.
topics.example: Code → Commit → Build → Test → Package → Deploy → Monitor → Feedback.
topics.mistake: Assuming every organisation uses the same stage names or needs the same amount of automation.
topics.recap: A pipeline is valuable when it creates repeatable evidence and useful feedback.

topics.title: Cloud-native, GitOps, AIOps, and DevSecOps
topics.definition: These are modern practices that extend DevOps into cloud operations, configuration reconciliation, security, and operational data analysis.
topics.why: They help teams solve specific scaling, safety, and visibility problems when used intentionally.
topics.how: Cloud-native uses managed services and portable workloads; GitOps stores desired state in Git; AIOps groups patterns in operational data; DevSecOps shifts security left and keeps it shared.
topics.example: An Argo CD agent notices that a Kubernetes deployment differs from the version in Git and reconciles it.
topics.mistake: Treating a trend name as a guaranteed shortcut. The practice still needs clear ownership and a problem worth solving.
topics.recap: Modern practices are useful when they make a real system safer, clearer, or easier to operate.

topics.title: Challenges and solutions in adopting DevOps
topics.definition: Adoption means changing how a team plans, builds, releases, and learns from software in production.
topics.why: Most delivery problems are caused by unclear process and ownership, not a lack of tool choices.
topics.how: Start with one service, automate a painful repeatable task, add version control and tests, define ownership, and measure outcomes.
topics.example: A team can begin by making one deployment repeatable and adding a rollback note before redesigning the entire platform.
topics.mistake: Trying to fix isolated teams, unreliable tests, and manual work all at once.
topics.recap: Small, measured improvements create the trust needed for larger changes.

title: Cloud and Virtualization
description: Compare cloud service models, virtual machines, containers, serverless, and safe first steps on AWS.

topics.title: IaaS, PaaS, and SaaS
topics.definition: Cloud computing provides computing resources over a network on demand. IaaS rents infrastructure, PaaS manages more of the runtime, and SaaS delivers a complete application.
topics.why: Knowing the service model tells you how much of the stack your team must maintain.
topics.how: Move from IaaS to SaaS and the provider manages more of the operating system, runtime, and application surface.
topics.example: A virtual machine is IaaS; a managed application platform is PaaS; an online document editor is SaaS.
topics.mistake: Assuming more managed always means better. Control, cost, compliance, and operational effort still matter.
topics.recap: Choose the service model that gives the right balance of control and convenience.

topics.title: AWS, Azure, and Google Cloud overview
topics.definition: AWS, Microsoft Azure, and Google Cloud all provide compute, networking, storage, identity, databases, and monitoring.
topics.why: Cloud concepts transfer between providers even when product names and defaults differ.
topics.how: Compare equivalent building blocks such as virtual machines, object storage, virtual networks, identity permissions, and managed Kubernetes.
topics.example: This course uses AWS for hands-on practice while mapping the same concepts to Azure and Google Cloud.
topics.mistake: Choosing a provider only because of popularity. Requirements, cost, skills, compliance, and support should guide the choice.
topics.recap: Learn the concept first, then the provider-specific product name.

topics.title: Virtual machines, containers, and serverless
topics.definition: A VM runs a guest operating system, a container packages an app while sharing the host kernel, and serverless hides much infrastructure management.
topics.why: The execution model changes isolation, startup time, cost, and operational responsibility.
topics.how: Use VMs for OS-level control, containers for repeatable packaging, and serverless when its limits fit the workload.
topics.example: A small web API may run in a container while a scheduled image resize runs as a serverless function.
topics.mistake: Thinking serverless means no servers exist. It means the provider operates more of them for you.
topics.recap: Match the runtime model to the workload and the team’s operational capacity.

topics.title: Public, private, hybrid, and multi-cloud
topics.definition: Deployment models describe where cloud infrastructure is hosted and how organisations combine environments.
topics.why: The model affects control, connectivity, cost, compliance, and complexity.
topics.how: Public cloud is provider infrastructure; private cloud is dedicated; hybrid connects private and public; multi-cloud uses more than one provider.
topics.example: A regulated workload may stay on private infrastructure while burst capacity runs in a public cloud.
topics.mistake: Assuming multi-cloud is automatically cheaper or more resilient.
topics.recap: Cloud architecture is a set of trade-offs, not a badge of maturity.

topics.title: Setting up cloud resources safely
topics.definition: A safe cloud lab uses least privilege, a selected region, tags, cost alerts, and a cleanup plan.
topics.why: Cloud resources can incur charges and weak credentials can expose data.
topics.how: Use an appropriate IAM identity, start with a small resource, inspect networking, monitor cost, and delete resources when the lab ends.
topics.example: Create a tagged test instance in one region, record its purpose, then terminate it after the exercise.
topics.mistake: Using root credentials or leaving test resources running.
topics.recap: Cloud learning includes cost, identity, and cleanup discipline.

title: Linux Fundamentals
description: Build a dependable command-line foundation, from files and permissions to processes, shell scripts, and remote access.

topics.title: Linux and distributions
topics.definition: Linux is an open-source kernel used by many operating systems. A distribution packages the kernel with tools, libraries, package management, and defaults.
topics.why: Distributions shape commands, package names, update tools, and support expectations.
topics.how: Ubuntu and Debian often use APT; Fedora and RHEL-family systems commonly use DNF. Core shell ideas remain portable.
topics.example: A command may be the same on Ubuntu and Fedora while the package manager command differs.
topics.mistake: Assuming every distribution behaves exactly the same.
topics.recap: Learn the common shell model and check the distribution’s documentation for differences.

topics.title: The Linux file system
topics.definition: Linux presents files, devices, and many system resources through one directory tree starting at `/`.
topics.why: Knowing where configuration, logs, user files, and programs live makes troubleshooting faster.
topics.how: `/home` stores users, `/etc` stores configuration, `/var/log` stores many logs, `/usr` holds programs, and `/tmp` holds temporary files.
topics.example: Use `pwd` to locate yourself and `ls -la` to inspect the current directory.
topics.mistake: Running a destructive command before checking the path.
topics.recap: Paths are context. Always confirm where you are before changing or deleting files.

topics.title: Basic Linux commands
topics.definition: Commands such as `pwd`, `ls`, `whoami`, `date`, `man`, and `clear` help you inspect and navigate a system.
topics.why: Small commands build the mental model needed for safe automation.
topics.how: Use `command --help` and manual pages to learn options instead of memorising every flag.
topics.example: `pwd && ls -la` prints your location and the files around you.
topics.mistake: Copying flags without understanding their effect.
topics.recap: Inspect first, then change. The shell rewards careful, observable steps.

topics.title: Users, groups, permissions, and ownership
topics.definition: Every file has an owner, group, and permissions for user, group, and others.
topics.why: Permissions protect services and data from accidental or unauthorised access.
topics.how: `r`, `w`, and `x` represent read, write, and execute. `chmod` changes permissions and `chown` changes ownership.
topics.example: Numeric mode `755` gives the owner read/write/execute and everyone else read/execute.
topics.mistake: Using `777` as a routine fix because it hides the real ownership problem.
topics.recap: Prefer individual accounts, least privilege, and the smallest permission change that works.

topics.title: Processes, services, monitoring, and logs
topics.definition: Processes are running programs; services are managed workloads; logs are records of system and application events.
topics.why: Together they show what is running, how resources are behaving, and what changed.
topics.how: Use `ps`, `top`, `systemctl`, `free -h`, `df -h`, `ss`, and log tools to gather evidence before acting.
topics.example: Check `systemctl status nginx`, then inspect recent logs before restarting a service.
topics.mistake: Restarting or killing a process blindly on a shared or production system.
topics.recap: Observe symptoms, correlate evidence, and choose the least disruptive action.

title: Version Control with Git and GitHub/GitLab
description: Learn the everyday Git workflow, collaboration patterns, branching strategies, and practical GitHub habits.
recordings: Git merge conflict, branching and strategies

topics.title: Git fundamentals
topics.definition: Git records changes to files as a local history of commits.
topics.why: A clear history makes work reviewable, reversible, and easier to share.
topics.how: Initialise or clone a repository, stage intentional changes, commit a message, then push and pull with a remote.
topics.example: `git add app.js && git commit -m "Add health check"` records one focused change.
topics.mistake: Committing generated secrets or mixing unrelated changes into one commit.
topics.recap: Keep commits small, descriptive, and safe to share.

topics.title: Branching, merging, and rebasing
topics.definition: Branches are movable names that let work progress separately before histories are combined.
topics.why: Branches let a team review changes without destabilising the main line.
topics.how: Create a branch, make commits, open a review, and merge after checks pass. Rebase only when the history rewrite is understood.
topics.example: A feature branch can be updated from `main` before a pull request is merged.
topics.mistake: Rewriting shared history without agreement.
topics.recap: Use branches to isolate change and use review to build shared confidence.

topics.title: Remote repositories and collaboration
topics.definition: A remote repository is a shared copy hosted by a service such as GitHub or GitLab.
topics.why: Remote collaboration gives a team one place for review, automation, and release history.
topics.how: Push branches, open pull or merge requests, respond to feedback, and protect the main branch with required checks.
topics.example: A pull request links code review, CI results, and the decision to merge.
topics.mistake: Treating a remote as a backup only; it is also a communication surface.
topics.recap: Healthy collaboration keeps code, context, and checks close together.

topics.title: GitFlow, trunk-based development, and CI
topics.definition: Git workflows are agreements about branch lifetime, release timing, and how changes reach production.
topics.why: A shared workflow reduces merge surprises and keeps delivery predictable.
topics.how: GitFlow uses longer-lived release branches; trunk-based development keeps changes close to the main branch with strong automation.
topics.example: Small changes behind a feature flag can merge to trunk while the feature is still being completed.
topics.mistake: Copying a workflow without matching it to the team’s release cadence.
topics.recap: The best workflow makes the safe path the easy path.

title: Continuous Integration (CI)
description: Connect source control to repeatable builds, test automation, Jenkins pipelines, and GitHub Actions workflows.
recordings: RBAC part 2 and pipeline stage view

topics.title: CI concepts and benefits
topics.definition: Continuous Integration means merging small changes often and validating them automatically.
topics.why: Frequent checks reduce the time between a mistake and its discovery.
topics.how: A CI job checks out code, installs dependencies, builds, tests, and publishes useful evidence.
topics.example: Every pull request runs unit tests before a reviewer approves it.
topics.mistake: Calling a scheduled nightly build CI while changes wait all day for feedback.
topics.recap: Good CI is frequent, repeatable, fast enough to use, and trusted by the team.

topics.title: Jenkins pipelines and agents
topics.definition: Jenkins is an automation server that runs pipeline stages on workers called agents.
topics.why: It can coordinate repeatable build, test, and deployment workflows across environments.
topics.how: A pipeline declares stages, credentials boundaries, agents, and post-build reporting.
topics.example: A pipeline can build an artifact on one agent and run integration tests on another.
topics.mistake: Giving every job broad credentials or installing plugins without ownership.
topics.recap: Pipelines should be readable, least-privileged, and easy to rerun.

topics.title: GitHub Actions and GitLab CI/CD
topics.definition: Hosted CI platforms run declarative workflows in response to repository events.
topics.why: Workflow files keep automation close to the code that needs it.
topics.how: Define triggers, jobs, runners, steps, caches, artifacts, and protected secrets in YAML.
topics.example: A pull request workflow can lint code and publish a test report without deploying.
topics.mistake: Hard-coding secrets or letting deployment jobs run on every branch.
topics.recap: Use event rules and environments to make automation deliberate.

topics.title: Maven and Gradle build automation
topics.definition: Maven and Gradle manage Java project dependencies, compilation, tests, and packaging.
topics.why: A consistent build tool turns local steps into repeatable CI work.
topics.how: The build file describes plugins, dependencies, tasks, and output artifacts.
topics.example: A CI job can run `./gradlew test` or `mvn test` and archive the result.
topics.mistake: Letting local machine state hide missing dependencies or version differences.
topics.recap: Pin versions where practical and make the build reproducible from a clean runner.

topics.title: Automated testing integration
topics.definition: Automated tests check behavior without requiring a person to repeat the same steps manually.
topics.why: Tests make frequent change safer and provide evidence for review and release.
topics.how: Run fast unit tests early, integration tests when dependencies are available, and publish clear failure output.
topics.example: A failing API contract test can stop a deployment before it reaches a shared environment.
topics.mistake: Measuring success by test count rather than useful coverage and trustworthy feedback.
topics.recap: Automate the checks that protect important behavior and keep failures actionable.

title: Containers and Containerization
description: Understand container images, lifecycle, networking, storage, Compose, and daemonless alternatives.

topics.title: Images, containers, and Dockerfiles
topics.definition: An image is a packaged filesystem and metadata; a container is a running instance of an image.
topics.why: Packaging dependencies makes applications easier to move between environments.
topics.how: A Dockerfile describes build steps, then the image runs with a command and limited resources.
topics.example: Build a small image, run it on a local port, and inspect the logs.
topics.mistake: Putting secrets into image layers or using a large unpinned base image.
topics.recap: Treat images as build artifacts and containers as replaceable runtime instances.

topics.title: Container lifecycle and best practices
topics.definition: Containers can be created, started, stopped, inspected, and removed as part of a controlled lifecycle.
topics.why: Lifecycle discipline avoids orphaned processes, surprise state, and confusing debugging.
topics.how: Keep containers focused, log to standard output, define health checks, and rebuild instead of patching a running container.
topics.example: A failed container is replaced from the same image after the root cause is fixed.
topics.mistake: Treating a container like a long-lived VM with hand-edited state.
topics.recap: Immutable build artifacts and observable runtime behavior are the safer default.

topics.title: Networking and storage
topics.definition: Container networking connects workloads; volumes and bind mounts provide data outside a container’s writable layer.
topics.why: Applications need predictable connectivity and data that survives replacement.
topics.how: Use named networks for service discovery and explicit volumes for stateful data.
topics.example: An API connects to a database by service name on a private Compose network.
topics.mistake: Exposing every internal port to the host or storing important data only in the container layer.
topics.recap: Make boundaries explicit: who can connect, and where data lives.

topics.title: Docker Compose for multi-container applications
topics.definition: Compose describes related services, networks, volumes, and environment settings in one file.
topics.why: It makes a local multi-service environment repeatable for a team.
topics.how: Define services, dependencies, health checks, and safe environment placeholders in YAML.
topics.example: A web service and database can start together with one Compose command.
topics.mistake: Checking real passwords into a Compose file.
topics.recap: Compose is a development and test convenience; production still needs an operated platform.

topics.title: Podman and Buildah
topics.definition: Podman runs containers without a central daemon and Buildah builds images with a daemonless workflow.
topics.why: Different environments may prefer rootless or daemonless tooling.
topics.how: Use compatible image formats and test the same application lifecycle across tools.
topics.example: A rootless Podman container can run a local service without a privileged daemon.
topics.mistake: Assuming every Docker-specific flag or integration behaves identically.
topics.recap: Learn the container model first, then check tool-specific behavior.

title: Container Orchestration
description: Move from one container to reliable clusters with Kubernetes workloads, services, configuration, and packaging.

topics.title: Kubernetes fundamentals
topics.definition: Kubernetes is a control system that schedules and reconciles container workloads across a cluster.
topics.why: It helps teams declare the desired state of applications and automate recovery and rollout.
topics.how: You submit objects to the API; controllers compare desired and actual state and act to close the gap.
topics.example: A Deployment keeps a requested number of web Pods running.
topics.mistake: Treating Kubernetes as a magic fix for an unclear application architecture.
topics.recap: Kubernetes is powerful because of reconciliation, not because YAML is special.

topics.title: Control plane, workers, API server, and etcd
topics.definition: The control plane stores and coordinates cluster state while worker nodes run workloads.
topics.why: Architecture knowledge helps you reason about failures and responsibility.
topics.how: The API server is the entry point; controllers and schedulers make decisions; etcd stores state; nodes run workloads.
topics.example: A scheduler selects a suitable worker for a new Pod.
topics.mistake: Assuming the control plane and application containers have the same failure domain.
topics.recap: Know which component stores state, makes decisions, and runs workloads.

topics.title: Pods and ReplicaSets
topics.definition: A Pod is Kubernetes’ smallest deployable unit; a ReplicaSet keeps a set of matching Pods running.
topics.why: Pods model co-located containers, while ReplicaSets provide basic availability.
topics.how: Labels connect a ReplicaSet’s selector to the Pods it should manage.
topics.example: A ReplicaSet can replace a failed Pod so the desired count remains three.
topics.mistake: Treating a Pod as a permanent server identity.
topics.recap: Pods are replaceable; persistent identity needs a different workload pattern.

topics.title: Deployments and StatefulSets
topics.definition: Deployments manage stateless rolling updates; StatefulSets provide stable identity and ordered behavior for stateful workloads.
topics.why: The workload controller should match how the application stores and uses state.
topics.how: Deployments create ReplicaSets and roll versions; StatefulSets manage stable names, storage claims, and ordered changes.
topics.example: A web frontend uses a Deployment while a database cluster may need a StatefulSet.
topics.mistake: Putting stateful software in a generic Deployment without a storage and backup plan.
topics.recap: Choose the controller from the workload’s identity and data needs.

topics.title: Services, networking, and Ingress
topics.definition: A Service gives a stable network identity to changing Pods; Ingress routes external HTTP traffic.
topics.why: Clients should not need to know individual Pod addresses.
topics.how: Selectors connect Services to Pods, while an Ingress controller applies hostname and path rules.
topics.example: `api.example.test` can route to a Service that balances traffic across API Pods.
topics.mistake: Publishing internal services broadly when a private ClusterIP would be enough.
topics.recap: Stable service boundaries keep workloads replaceable and clients simple.

title: Infrastructure as Code (IaC)
description: Turn infrastructure into repeatable, reviewable configuration with Terraform providers, state, and modules.

topics.title: Infrastructure automation concepts
topics.definition: Infrastructure as Code describes infrastructure with files that can be reviewed, tested, and applied repeatedly.
topics.why: Declarative configuration reduces manual drift and makes changes visible.
topics.how: A plan shows the difference between desired configuration and observed infrastructure before an apply changes anything.
topics.example: A pull request can show that one test instance will be added before the team approves it.
topics.mistake: Applying changes without reviewing the plan or protecting state.
topics.recap: IaC creates an auditable change path for infrastructure.

topics.title: Providers, resources, state, and modules
topics.definition: Terraform uses providers to talk to APIs, resources to describe objects, state to map them, and modules to reuse patterns.
topics.why: These pieces explain what Terraform knows and what it will change.
topics.how: Configuration declares resources; Terraform compares them to state and provider observations.
topics.example: An AWS provider can manage a VPC resource through a reusable networking module.
topics.mistake: Treating state as disposable or editing it casually.
topics.recap: State is an important operational record and needs secure storage and access control.

topics.title: Writing and applying Terraform configurations
topics.definition: The Terraform workflow commonly uses format, validate, plan, apply, and destroy commands.
topics.why: Each step catches a different class of mistake and makes change more deliberate.
topics.how: Format and validate locally, inspect the plan, apply in the intended workspace, and record outputs.
topics.example: `terraform plan` is evidence for a review; `terraform apply` performs the approved change.
topics.mistake: Running apply from the wrong account, region, or workspace.
topics.recap: Context checks are as important as syntax checks.

topics.title: Pulumi overview
topics.definition: Pulumi is an infrastructure tool that lets teams define resources with general-purpose languages.
topics.why: Using familiar languages can help teams share abstractions and testing patterns.
topics.how: Pulumi programs create resources through provider SDKs and store deployment state.
topics.example: A TypeScript program can define a cloud bucket and export its URL.
topics.mistake: Assuming a programming language removes the need to reason about infrastructure state.
topics.recap: Different IaC tools share the same need for safe plans, state, and ownership.

topics.title: Integrating IaC into CI/CD
topics.definition: IaC in CI/CD means proposing, validating, and applying infrastructure through controlled automation.
topics.why: It reduces manual access and creates a review trail for changes.
topics.how: Run formatting and validation on every change, create a plan on review, and restrict applies to protected environments.
topics.example: A merge to the infrastructure main branch can trigger a reviewed plan and a gated apply.
topics.mistake: Letting any branch apply production infrastructure.
topics.recap: Separate preview from apply and keep production permissions narrow.

title: Configuration Management
description: Make host configuration repeatable with Ansible concepts, YAML, roles, variables, and safe automation.

topics.title: Ansible inventories, playbooks, and roles
topics.definition: Ansible describes desired host configuration in inventories, playbooks, tasks, and reusable roles.
topics.why: Repeatable configuration reduces the drift created by manual server changes.
topics.how: An inventory names hosts, a playbook maps tasks to them, and roles package reusable behavior.
topics.example: A playbook can install Nginx, copy a safe config template, and ensure the service is enabled.
topics.mistake: Running a playbook with an overly broad inventory.
topics.recap: Start with a small inventory and make each task understandable and idempotent.

topics.title: YAML syntax and structure
topics.definition: YAML is a human-readable data format often used for automation configuration.
topics.why: Indentation and data types control how tools interpret the file.
topics.how: Use spaces, consistent nesting, quoted values when needed, and a linter before automation runs.
topics.example: A list of packages is represented as indented entries below a key.
topics.mistake: Using tabs or assuming every unquoted value is a string.
topics.recap: Readable YAML is safer YAML; validate before you execute.

topics.title: Galaxy, handlers, and variables
topics.definition: Ansible Galaxy shares roles; handlers run when notified; variables keep values configurable.
topics.why: Reuse and explicit change triggers keep automation shorter and safer.
topics.how: A task notifies a handler when configuration changes, while variables separate policy from implementation.
topics.example: Restart Nginx only when its configuration template changes.
topics.mistake: Restarting every service on every run.
topics.recap: Idempotence means the second run should make no unnecessary change.

topics.title: Automating infrastructure with Ansible
topics.definition: Ansible can configure hosts, deploy applications, and coordinate repeatable operational steps.
topics.why: Automation creates a repeatable path for common operations and recovery.
topics.how: Use check mode, limit flags, inventories, and versioned playbooks before changing important systems.
topics.example: Run a playbook against one canary host before a wider rollout.
topics.mistake: Skipping a dry run because a playbook succeeded last week.
topics.recap: Controlled scope and observable output make automation trustworthy.

topics.title: Puppet and Chef comparison
topics.definition: Puppet and Chef are configuration-management tools with their own models, ecosystems, and operational patterns.
topics.why: Tool choice affects team skills, control planes, and long-term maintenance.
topics.how: Compare pull or push behavior, language, agent model, inventory, and community support against the actual environment.
topics.example: A team may prefer one tool because it fits an existing compliance workflow.
topics.mistake: Choosing by popularity without considering operational fit.
topics.recap: The transferable skill is safe, repeatable configuration management.

title: Continuous Delivery and Deployment
description: Ship with confidence using progressive delivery patterns, GitOps workflows, and Kubernetes deployment automation.

topics.title: Continuous Delivery vs Continuous Deployment
topics.definition: Continuous Delivery keeps changes ready for release; Continuous Deployment automatically releases changes after checks pass.
topics.why: The distinction makes approval points and risk ownership explicit.
topics.how: Both rely on repeatable pipelines, but deployment removes a manual release decision when confidence is high enough.
topics.example: A regulated service may use continuous delivery with a human approval gate.
topics.mistake: Treating automatic deployment as the only measure of delivery maturity.
topics.recap: Choose the release policy that matches risk and evidence.

topics.title: Blue-green, canary, and rolling deployments
topics.definition: Progressive delivery changes how new versions receive traffic so risk is limited and rollback is practical.
topics.why: Small exposure windows make failures easier to detect and contain.
topics.how: Blue-green switches between environments; canary sends a small share of traffic; rolling updates replace instances gradually.
topics.example: Send 5% of traffic to a canary and compare errors before increasing it.
topics.mistake: Calling a rollout progressive without monitoring or a rollback path.
topics.recap: A strategy is only safe when signals and rollback are ready.

topics.title: GitOps with Argo CD and Flux CD
topics.definition: GitOps stores desired system configuration in Git and uses a reconciler to keep the runtime aligned.
topics.why: Git provides reviewable history, while reconciliation reduces manual drift.
topics.how: A controller watches Git, compares desired state with the cluster, and applies changes according to policy.
topics.example: A version bump merged to a deployment repository becomes the next cluster release.
topics.mistake: Allowing unreviewed manual changes to become the hidden source of truth.
topics.recap: GitOps works when repository permissions and cluster ownership are clear.

topics.title: Integrating deployments with Kubernetes
topics.definition: Kubernetes deployment automation updates workload objects, waits for health, and reports rollout status.
topics.why: The platform needs evidence that the new version is running, not just that a YAML file changed.
topics.how: Apply a versioned manifest or chart, observe rollout status, verify service health, and keep a rollback command ready.
topics.example: A rollout can pause when readiness probes fail and preserve the last healthy version.
topics.mistake: Skipping readiness checks because Pods reached Running state.
topics.recap: Running is not the same as ready; release automation needs application-level signals.

title: Monitoring, Logging, and Observability
description: Use metrics, logs, traces, and alerting to understand system behavior and respond to incidents.

topics.title: Why monitoring matters
topics.definition: Monitoring collects signals about system health, performance, and behavior over time.
topics.why: Without signals, teams discover failure from user reports and have little evidence for diagnosis.
topics.how: Choose service-level indicators, collect them consistently, and connect alerts to human action.
topics.example: Track request latency, error rate, and traffic for an API.
topics.mistake: Alerting on every noisy metric without a clear response.
topics.recap: A signal is useful when it changes a decision.

topics.title: Prometheus and Grafana
topics.definition: Prometheus stores time-series metrics; Grafana visualizes metrics and other data sources in dashboards.
topics.why: Together they make trends and regressions easier to see.
topics.how: Expose metrics, scrape them, write focused queries, and build panels around user and service outcomes.
topics.example: A dashboard can show request rate, p95 latency, and error percentage on one service row.
topics.mistake: Building decorative dashboards with no owner or action.
topics.recap: Dashboards should support a question, not just display data.

topics.title: ELK and EFK logging stacks
topics.definition: Centralized logging collects application and infrastructure logs so they can be searched and correlated.
topics.why: Distributed systems make it difficult to diagnose issues from one machine.
topics.how: Ship structured logs, parse them, index useful fields, control retention, and restrict access.
topics.example: Search logs by request ID to follow one user action across services.
topics.mistake: Logging secrets or unlimited high-cardinality data.
topics.recap: Structured, minimal, searchable logs reduce investigation time.

topics.title: Tracing with Jaeger and OpenTelemetry
topics.definition: Tracing follows a request across services with spans and timing data.
topics.why: Traces show where time is spent when logs and metrics cannot explain a distributed delay.
topics.how: Instrument services, propagate context, sample intentionally, and protect trace data.
topics.example: A trace can show that an API delay came from a slow database call.
topics.mistake: Collecting every trace forever without a cost or privacy plan.
topics.recap: Use traces to answer path and timing questions across boundaries.

topics.title: Alerting and incident management
topics.definition: An alert is a signal that should prompt a person or system to act; incident management coordinates response and learning.
topics.why: Reliable response needs clear ownership, severity, and communication.
topics.how: Define thresholds around impact, route alerts, document runbooks, and review incidents without blame.
topics.example: A sustained error budget burn can page the on-call engineer with a rollback runbook.
topics.mistake: Paging people for symptoms that do not require immediate action.
topics.recap: Good alerts are actionable, owned, and connected to learning.

title: DevSecOps
description: Build security into delivery with scanning, secrets management, policy as code, and shared responsibility.

topics.title: Security fundamentals in CI/CD
topics.definition: DevSecOps integrates security checks and shared security responsibility into development and delivery.
topics.why: Finding a weakness earlier usually reduces the cost and disruption of fixing it.
topics.how: Threat-model important paths, protect build systems, scan dependencies, and treat findings according to risk.
topics.example: A pull request check can block a known critical dependency vulnerability.
topics.mistake: Making security a final gate owned by one team only.
topics.recap: Security is a delivery capability, not a separate handoff.

topics.title: Vulnerability scanning with Trivy
topics.definition: Vulnerability scanners compare packages, images, and files with databases of known issues.
topics.why: Scanning helps teams see risk before software reaches users.
topics.how: Scan at the right stages, set severity policy, review false positives, and update the scanner database.
topics.example: Scan a container image before pushing it to a registry.
topics.mistake: Treating a clean scan as proof that no risk exists.
topics.recap: Scanning is one signal within a wider security process.

topics.title: Secrets management
topics.definition: Secrets are sensitive values such as tokens, passwords, and private keys that should not live in source code.
topics.why: Exposed secrets can grant direct access to data and infrastructure.
topics.how: Use a managed secret store, least privilege, rotation, short-lived credentials, and redaction in logs.
topics.example: A deployment retrieves a database password at runtime from a secret manager.
topics.mistake: Putting a real key in a private repository and assuming it is safe.
topics.recap: Keep secrets out of code, logs, URLs, and screenshots.

topics.title: SAST, DAST, and dependency scanning
topics.definition: SAST checks source, DAST tests a running application, and dependency scanning checks third-party packages.
topics.why: Different tools find different classes of weakness.
topics.how: Use them at appropriate pipeline stages and triage findings with context.
topics.example: A DAST job tests a deployed preview while SAST scans the pull request.
topics.mistake: Treating tool output as a substitute for security review.
topics.recap: Layered checks improve coverage, but people still make decisions.

topics.title: Compliance and policy as code
topics.definition: Policy as code expresses rules in a testable, versioned format that automation can evaluate.
topics.why: Codified policy makes expectations repeatable and reviewable.
topics.how: Write a narrow rule, test it against fixtures, explain exceptions, and apply it at the right boundary.
topics.example: OPA can reject a workload that requests a privileged container.
topics.mistake: Writing opaque policies that teams cannot understand or safely change.
topics.recap: Good policy is explicit, testable, and connected to a real risk.

title: Collaboration and Project Management Tools
description: Coordinate work with Agile habits, planning tools, ChatOps, and documentation that stays close to delivery.

topics.title: Agile and Scrum overview
topics.definition: Agile is a set of values for learning through small increments; Scrum is one framework for organising that work.
topics.why: Short feedback cycles help teams adapt to what they learn.
topics.how: Plan a small goal, build and review an increment, then reflect on how the team can improve.
topics.example: A sprint review shows working software rather than a slide deck of future work.
topics.mistake: Using ceremonies without improving the flow of value.
topics.recap: Agile is about learning and delivery, not meeting volume.

topics.title: Jira, Azure Boards, and Trello
topics.definition: Project tools represent work, ownership, priority, and workflow state.
topics.why: Visible work helps a team coordinate and discuss trade-offs.
topics.how: Keep issue types simple, define clear states, link work to code, and archive what no longer matters.
topics.example: A ticket can link a pull request and release note while showing who owns the next step.
topics.mistake: Turning the board into a detailed inventory that nobody keeps current.
topics.recap: A board is useful when it helps the team make a decision.

topics.title: Slack, Teams, and ChatOps
topics.definition: ChatOps connects operational commands, alerts, and context to team communication channels.
topics.why: Shared context speeds coordination during routine work and incidents.
topics.how: Use named channels, clear permissions, command confirmations, and links back to source systems.
topics.example: A deployment bot posts the version, change owner, and health check to a release channel.
topics.mistake: Allowing privileged commands in a noisy channel without confirmation.
topics.recap: Chat can coordinate work, but source systems remain the source of truth.

topics.title: Confluence, Notion, and MkDocs
topics.definition: Documentation stores decisions, guides, and knowledge so the team does not rely on memory.
topics.why: Written context reduces repeated questions and makes onboarding possible.
topics.how: Keep pages close to their audience, date time-sensitive instructions, and link procedures to owners.
topics.example: An MkDocs site can publish a versioned runbook from a repository.
topics.mistake: Writing a page once and never checking whether the procedure still works.
topics.recap: Documentation is part of the product and needs maintenance.

title: AI/ML Ops: AIOps and MLOps
description: Understand how AI assists operations and how machine-learning systems need their own repeatable lifecycle.

topics.title: Introduction to AIOps and MLOps
topics.definition: AIOps uses data analysis and AI techniques for operations; MLOps applies delivery and operations discipline to machine-learning systems.
topics.why: Both areas address complexity, but they solve different problems and need careful evaluation.
topics.how: AIOps works with operational signals; MLOps manages data, models, experiments, deployment, and monitoring.
topics.example: An AIOps workflow groups related alerts while an MLOps workflow tracks which model version produced a prediction.
topics.mistake: Using AI language without defining the operational outcome.
topics.recap: Start with the problem, the data, and the decision that should improve.

topics.title: AI in DevOps
topics.definition: AI can help summarise incidents, suggest changes, detect patterns, and assist with repetitive engineering tasks.
topics.why: Used carefully, it can reduce toil while leaving important decisions with people.
topics.how: Give AI bounded context, review outputs, protect sensitive data, and measure whether it improves outcomes.
topics.example: A tool can draft a first incident summary from approved logs for an engineer to edit.
topics.mistake: Treating generated text as verified operational truth.
topics.recap: AI assistance needs guardrails, provenance, and human review.

topics.title: The machine-learning lifecycle
topics.definition: A machine-learning lifecycle includes data collection, preparation, training, evaluation, deployment, and monitoring.
topics.why: A model can change behavior when data or the real world changes.
topics.how: Version data and code, record experiments, evaluate against meaningful metrics, and observe predictions after release.
topics.example: A model is retrained when drift moves a monitored feature distribution beyond a threshold.
topics.mistake: Only versioning the model file and losing the data and code that created it.
topics.recap: Reproducibility and monitoring are core production requirements.

topics.title: ML pipelines and deployment
topics.definition: ML pipelines automate repeatable data and model steps while preserving artifacts and metadata.
topics.why: Automation makes training and release consistent enough to compare and audit.
topics.how: Validate data, train, evaluate, register, approve, deploy, and monitor a model through explicit stages.
topics.example: A pipeline blocks promotion when evaluation metrics fall below the approved baseline.
topics.mistake: Optimising training without testing inference behavior in production-like conditions.
topics.recap: ML delivery needs both statistical checks and software reliability checks.

topics.title: MLflow and Kubeflow
topics.definition: MLflow tracks experiments and model artifacts; Kubeflow provides Kubernetes-oriented tools for ML workflows.
topics.why: Tools help teams organise experiments and operate repeatable pipelines.
topics.how: Use tracking, registries, pipeline definitions, and deployment targets according to the team’s complexity.
topics.example: Register a candidate model with its metrics and dataset version before deployment.
topics.mistake: Adopting a platform before the team can describe its workflow.
topics.recap: Tooling should clarify the lifecycle, not obscure it.

topics.title: AI-powered monitoring and predictive incidents
topics.definition: AI-powered monitoring looks for patterns or anomalies in operational data to support investigation and prioritisation.
topics.why: It can help humans notice relationships across large volumes of signals.
topics.how: Define the signal quality, evaluate false positives, keep explanations available, and connect predictions to runbooks.
topics.example: A model highlights a cluster of unusual latency and deployment events for an engineer to review.
topics.mistake: Paging on a prediction without measuring its precision and response value.
topics.recap: Prediction is useful only when it improves a human or automated decision.

topics.title: Generative AI for DevOps engineers
topics.definition: Generative AI creates text, code, or summaries from prompts and context.
topics.why: It can accelerate drafts and exploration when inputs and outputs are handled safely.
topics.how: Use non-sensitive examples, ask for structured outputs, verify commands, and never paste private credentials.
topics.example: Ask for a draft CI checklist, then adapt it to the project’s actual requirements.
topics.mistake: Running generated infrastructure commands without reviewing them.
topics.recap: Treat generated output as a draft that needs engineering judgment.

title: Capstone: End-to-End DevOps Pipeline
description: Bring the curriculum together in a practical pipeline from Git commit to secure, observable Kubernetes delivery.
recordings: Kubernetes with Helm and Argo CD

topics.title: Project overview
topics.definition: The capstone is an end-to-end service delivery exercise that connects code, automation, infrastructure, deployment, security, and monitoring.
topics.why: Integration shows whether the concepts work together under realistic constraints.
topics.how: Start with a small service and make each stage observable, repeatable, and explainable.
topics.example: A simple web API is enough if the pipeline around it is reliable.
topics.mistake: Choosing a project so large that the delivery path never becomes complete.
topics.recap: The goal is a trustworthy path, not a giant feature list.

topics.title: Code in GitHub and add CI
topics.definition: The project repository stores source, documentation, workflow files, and the history of decisions.
topics.why: Versioned source is the starting point for collaboration and automation.
topics.how: Protect the main branch, add checks, and make the pipeline produce clear artifacts and test evidence.
topics.example: A pull request runs tests and builds the service before merge.
topics.mistake: Keeping deployment configuration outside the repository without documenting it.
topics.recap: A reviewer should be able to understand how code becomes a release.

topics.title: Build and containerize with Docker
topics.definition: Containerization packages the capstone service and its runtime dependencies into a repeatable artifact.
topics.why: The same artifact can move through environments with fewer surprises.
topics.how: Use a small base image, a non-root runtime where possible, health checks, and a clear version tag.
topics.example: The pipeline builds an image, scans it, and pushes it to a registry after tests pass.
topics.mistake: Using `latest` as the only release identifier.
topics.recap: Build artifacts should be reproducible, traceable, and safe to run.

topics.title: Deploy on Kubernetes with Helm and Argo CD
topics.definition: Helm packages Kubernetes resources; Argo CD reconciles desired deployment state from Git.
topics.why: Together they make environment changes reviewable and repeatable.
topics.how: Version a chart or manifests, update the desired image tag, review the diff, and observe the rollout.
topics.example: A merge updates the staging values file and Argo CD syncs the cluster.
topics.mistake: Allowing manual cluster edits to become the hidden source of truth.
topics.recap: The deployment repository and cluster should tell the same story.

topics.title: Monitor securely with Prometheus, Grafana, Trivy, and Vault
topics.definition: The capstone needs health signals and security checks that follow the service from build to runtime.
topics.why: A deployed service is not complete if the team cannot see or protect it.
topics.how: Add metrics and dashboards, scan the image, retrieve secrets safely, and define a response path for failures.
topics.example: A dashboard shows error rate while a Trivy check blocks a critical image vulnerability.
topics.mistake: Adding tools without documenting who acts on their output.
topics.recap: Operational signals and security controls should lead to clear action.

topics.title: Required deliverables and assessment
topics.definition: Assessment checks the working pipeline, written decisions, evidence, and the learner’s explanation of trade-offs.
topics.why: A good submission proves understanding, not just a successful command.
topics.how: Submit the repository, architecture note, pipeline evidence, deployment instructions, monitoring view, and a short retrospective.
topics.example: Include one failure scenario and explain how the pipeline or runbook handles it.
topics.mistake: Showing only the happy path.
topics.recap: Document what works, what could fail, and what you would improve next.
